overview.intro:
Chapter 93 covers **firearms** — pistols and revolvers, sporting shotguns and rifles, military weapons — **air guns, airsoft guns and paintball markers**, **gun parts and accessories**, **ammunition** of every kind, and **swords and bayonets**. Its **67 tariff lines** are mostly low: all ammunition and most military weapons are Free, shotguns pay 2.6%, pistols 14¢ each + 3%. **Rifles entered with a telescopic sight** pay a two-part rate — for example 3.1% on the value of the rifle + 13% on the value of the sight — so the importer declares both values.

The extra duty by country decides the cost. Since **July 24, 2026** goods from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff** on every line, with no exemption list for this chapter: **EU goods pay 10% in total**, Türkiye the base rate plus 12.5%, the UK plus 10%, **Brazil plus 37.5%** and China plus 20%; **USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico enter free**. Every firearm and cartridge also needs an **ATF import permit**, and **Russian firearms and ammunition are denied**. U.S. imports were **$3.86B in 2025**, led by Türkiye, the UK, Italy and Germany.

workedExamples.title: Pistols: Austria vs. Türkiye vs. Brazil vs. Israel
workedExamples.body: Twenty semiautomatic pistols worth $10,000. The base rate is 14¢ each + 3% = $302.80. From Austria (or Croatia, Czechia, Germany) the EU rule replaces it with 10% in total: **$1,000**. From Türkiye: $302.80 + 12.5% = **$1,552.80**. From Brazil: $302.80 + 37.5% = **$4,052.80**. From Israel under the FTA: 12.5% only, **$1,250**. The importer also owes the 10% excise tax when it sells them — a tax, not a customs duty.

workedExamples.title: A rifle with a telescopic sight
workedExamples.body: A centerfire rifle entered with its scope, $1,000 in all: the rifle $800 and the sight $200, each reported under its own statistical suffix (statistical note 1). Base rate: 3.1% × $800 + 13% × $200 = **$50.80**. From Türkiye the 12.5% Section 301 duty is on the full $1,000: **$175.80**. From Germany the EU rule takes the higher of $50.80 and 10% of $1,000: **$100**. The same rifle without a scope pays $24.80 at the base rate.

seo.shortDescription: What changed for HTS Chapter 93 firearms, gun parts and ammunition since January 2025: unchanged base rates, the IEEPA tariffs and their end, the Section 122 surcharge, the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies, the Brazil action, China List 4A, and the Russian firearms and ammunition import restrictions.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). All 67 Chapter 93 lines carry the same base rates in both.

What changed came on top of the base rate. In 2025 the IEEPA tariffs added 10%–25% on most suppliers' firearms and ammunition — 15% in total for EU goods, 15% extra for Türkiye and Israel, 20% for Taiwan, and 40% more for Brazil from August 6, 2025 — while USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico paid nothing extra. They **ended on February 24, 2026**, and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026**, goods from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5%** on every Chapter 93 line, with no exemption list for this chapter; **Brazil** pays 25% more (from July 22, 2026), and **China** also keeps its **7.5% List 4A duty** on 66 of the 67 lines.

Apart from duties, **firearms and ammunition made in or located in Russia cannot be permanently imported**: since September 7, 2021 ATF must deny import permits for them under a State Department sanction.
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 93 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies, the Brazil Section 301 tariff, China Section 301 List 4A, Russia's column 2 and 35% rates, the Nicaragua Section 301 phase-in, and the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended. No Section 232 product list names a Chapter 93 line, no Chapter 93 line is on the Canada Section 338 lists (U.S. note 51), and no antidumping or countervailing duty order covers a firearm, gun part or ammunition. Also listed: the import restrictions on Russian firearms and ammunition and the 2026 ATF and State Department rules on arms imports. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: No Chapter 93 base-rate changes
changes.detail: All 67 Chapter 93 lines carry the same General, FTA and Column 2 rates in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition, including the rifle-plus-telescopic-sight rates of 9301.90.30, 9303.30.40 and 9303.30.80; no line was added, split or renumbered.

changes.title: China Section 301 List 4A continues
changes.detail: USTR received requests to continue the 2018–2019 China Section 301 actions, so they stay in effect during the four-year review. For Chapter 93 this keeps +7.5% (9903.88.15) on every subheading except 9305.99.40, on top of the 12.5% 2026 action.

changes.title: State Department restates its arms-embargo country policies (ITAR 126.1)
changes.detail: The rule reorganizes 22 CFR 126.1 and says its policy of denial covers exports, reexports, retransfers and temporary imports of defense articles destined for or originating in the listed countries. Russia stays on the list (126.1(l)). Permanent imports of firearms and ammunition remain ATF's (27 CFR part 447).

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies cover every Chapter 93 line
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on all products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84): 12.5% for Türkiye, China, Israel and Brazil, 10% for the UK, Canada, Mexico and India. No Chapter 93 line is on the general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b)) or on any country exception list in note 52(j). EU and Taiwanese goods pay 10% in total and Japanese and Korean goods 12.5% in total; USMCA-qualifying goods are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94). FTA claims remove the base rate but not this duty; goods entered under Chapter 98, such as U.S. firearms returned (9801.00.10), do not pay it.

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on products of Brazil
changes.detail: 25% on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01) on all 67 Chapter 93 lines; none is on the note 50(a)(ii) exemption list. From July 24 the 12.5% 2026 action (9903.05.27) is added, for 37.5% on top of the base rate.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still apply.

changes.title: ATF proposes to treat customs-bonded warehouses like foreign-trade zones
changes.detail: ATF's import rules already exclude firearms brought into a foreign-trade zone from "importation". The proposed rule would add customs-bonded warehouses and drop the "for storage" condition; it would not change customs requirements. Comments closed August 6, 2026; no final rule has been published.

changes.title: ATF proposes to update its list of proscribed countries
changes.detail: ATF proposed to replace the country list in 27 CFR 447.52(a) with a reference to the State Department's list (22 CFR 126.1) and to drop Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Moldova, Turkmenistan, Ukraine and Uzbekistan from the firearms and ammunition denial list in 447.52(b), leaving only Russia. Comments closed July 6, 2026; no final rule has been published, so the current list still applies.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. No Chapter 93 line was on the product exemption list (9903.03.03), so every firearm, part and cartridge paid it. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt.

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: Extra 25% on products of India ended
changes.detail: Executive Order 14384 ended the additional 25% duty on products of India (9903.01.84) that had applied since August 27, 2025. India's 25% reciprocal duty continued until February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Nicaragua Section 301 tariff phases in from 2027
changes.detail: USTR's action on Nicaragua adds a duty on all Nicaraguan goods that do not originate under CAFTA-DR (9903.89.01): 0% in 2026, 10% from January 1, 2027 and 15% from January 1, 2028. It reaches every Chapter 93 line.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty cut to 10%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14357 lowered the IEEPA duty on products of China (9903.01.24) from 20% to 10%, so Chinese firearms, parts and ammunition paid 10% + 10% reciprocal + 7.5% List 4A on top of the base rate. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Extra 25% on products of India
changes.detail: Executive Order 14329 added 25% on Indian goods (9903.01.84) on top of the 25% reciprocal rate, for 50% in all on Indian gun parts, ammunition and swords. Ended February 7, 2026.

changes.title: Country-specific reciprocal rates replace the 10% baseline
changes.detail: Executive Order 14326 set each country's reciprocal rate: Türkiye, Israel, Japan and South Korea +15%; Taiwan +20%; India +25%; EU goods 15% in total; the UK and Brazil stayed at +10%. No Chapter 93 line was on the reciprocal-tariff exemption list. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional 40% on products of Brazil
changes.detail: Executive Order 14323 added 40% on Brazilian goods (9903.01.77) on top of the 10% reciprocal duty, for 50% extra on Brazilian pistols, shotguns and ammunition. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods to +35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China reciprocal duty cut from 125% to 10%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14298 cut the reciprocal duty on Chinese goods to 10% for goods entered from May 14, 2025, so Chinese firearms, parts and ammunition paid 37.5% on top of the base rate (20% fentanyl + 10% + 7.5% List 4A). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China reciprocal duty raised to 125%; other country rates paused
changes.detail: Executive Order 14266 raised the reciprocal duty on Chinese goods to 125% and paused the higher country rates for other countries, leaving the 10% baseline. With the 20% fentanyl duty and List 4A, Chinese air guns, gun parts and ammunition paid 152.5% on top of the base rate until May 13, 2025.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) from April 5, 2025 and country rates (9903.02.xx); Canada and Mexico excluded. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty raised to 20%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14228 raised the IEEPA duty on products of China from 10% to 20%. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.01) from March 4, 2025; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.04). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Canada
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.10) from March 4, 2025, later raised to +35%; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.14). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of China
changes.detail: +10% on all goods of China (9903.01.20) from February 4, 2025, on top of the 7.5% List 4A duty. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Russian firearms and ammunition: ATF must deny import permits
changes.detail: Under the second round of Chemical and Biological Weapons Act sanctions on Russia, new or pending ATF permit applications to permanently import firearms or ammunition (U.S. Munitions Import List Categories I and III) manufactured or located in Russia are denied. The State Department said the measures stay in place for at least one year and until further notice; ATF's regulation already barred most Russian firearms under a 1996 agreement (27 CFR 447.52(b)).

changes.title: China List 4A cut from 15% to 7.5%
changes.detail: Under the U.S.-China Phase One agreement USTR halved the List 4A duty (9903.88.15) on Chinese firearms, gun parts, ammunition and swords.

changes.title: China List 4A: 15% on Chinese arms and ammunition
changes.detail: USTR's fourth China Section 301 list (9903.88.15) put 15% on every Chapter 93 subheading except 9305.99.40 from September 1, 2019. Cut to 7.5% from February 14, 2020.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 93 goods fell from **$4.45B in 2024 to $3.86B in 2025** (−13.3%), below every year since 2020 and well under the 2021 peak of $5.57B. **Ammunition is the largest group** at $1.34B (35%): other ammunition and parts (9306.90, $759M, +16%), rifle and pistol cartridges (9306.30, $468M, down from $827M) and shotgun cartridges ($71M). **Pistols and revolvers** were $660M (−19%), **sporting shotguns** $347M and **rifles** $254M. **Gun parts** were $1.02B — parts of military weapons $363M, of shotguns and rifles $319M, of pistols $268M — and air guns $171M.

Supply is spread out. **Türkiye** led with $419M (shotguns and rifles $156M, pistols $118M, ammunition $88M), then the **UK** $389M (ammunition $195M, parts $159M), **Italy** $366M (−23%, mostly shotguns and rifles), **Germany** $318M (ammunition $161M), **Austria** $249M (pistols $189M), **Canada** $247M (ammunition $154M) and **Brazil** $203M (−37%). Croatia ($102M) ships almost only pistols and Czechia ($137M) pistols and ammunition; Taiwan and China ship mostly air guns and parts. Imports from **Russia** fell from $183M in 2021 to $66M in 2022 and under $0.3M a year since; ATF has had to deny permits for Russian firearms and ammunition since September 7, 2021.

Through 2025 most of these goods paid the IEEPA duties — 15% in total for EU goods, 15% more for Türkiye and Israel, 50% more for Brazil from August 6 — while USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico paid nothing extra. Those duties ended on February 24, 2026; since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 tariff of 10% or 12.5% applies instead. 2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data.

industryAreas.intro:
The total rate on Chapter 93 goods depends on **where they come from** as much as on what they are. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference — computed from the current tariff schedule with the same engine as the tariff calculator.

Since the IEEPA duties ended on February 24, 2026, the extra duty is mainly the **Section 301 tariff on 60 economies** (from July 24, 2026), and no Chapter 93 line is on an exemption list. **EU goods** — Austrian, Czech, Croatian and German pistols, Italian and Spanish shotguns — pay **10% in total**; **Türkiye pays the base rate plus 12.5%**, the UK plus 10%, **Brazil plus 37.5%** and **China plus 20%**. **USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico enter free.** Rifles entered with a telescopic sight are shown with their two-part base rate, as the schedule prints it.

assumptions: Each total was computed by the official-measures calculator engine (the same data as the tariff calculator: measures.json, HTSUS 2026 Revision 21) for goods entered on 2026-10-13, priced on a $10,000 shipment and 1,000 units for per-unit rates.
Ranges like "Free · 11.8%" mean the group has lines with different base rates; select a cell to see which lines carry which rate.
A per-unit rate plus a percentage cannot be added into one number without the shipment’s weight, count or volume, so it is shown as written.
Preferences: USMCA (S) is applied for Canada and Mexico on the "USMCA-qualifying" side; IL for Israel. GSP (A, A+) has lapsed and is not applied. Other preferences are not applied.
Any other country shows the range across every country not listed (column 2 countries — Cuba, North Korea, Russia, Belarus — aside), without preferences.
The IEEPA duties (9903.01.xx, 9903.02.xx) are still printed in the schedule but ended February 24, 2026, and the Section 122 surcharge (9903.03.01) expired July 23, 2026; neither is applied.

Rifles with a telescopic sight (9301.90.30, 9303.30.40, 9303.30.80) are shown with the schedule's wording: the base rate is charged on the declared value of the rifle and of the sight (chapter 93 statistical note 1), so it can't be one number without those values. The extra duty is charged on the full customs value; the EU, Japan, Korea and Taiwan floors compare it with the two-part base rate.

Pistols and revolvers (9302) carry 14¢ each + 3%: the grid shows the per-unit part as written. Under the EU, Japan, Korea and Taiwan rules the 10%/12.5% total is higher than the base rate for any pistol worth more than a few dollars.
Russia is not in the grid: its goods take column 2 rates (35% on four subheadings) plus 12.5%, but ATF must deny permits to import firearms and ammunition made in or located in Russia.

Not in the grid: ATF import permits (Form 6) and import criteria, the State Department's arms-embargo rules, and the federal excise tax on firearms and ammunition (10% or 11% of the importer's sale price, 26 U.S.C. 4181), which is not a customs duty. See Import documents.

tariffEngineering.h1: Importing Firearms, Gun Parts & Ammunition (HTS Ch. 93): Permits, Rules & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Firearms & Ammunition: ATF Form 6, ITAR, Excise Tax & Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 93) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The rules for each HTS Chapter 93 line — ATF import permits (Form 6, 27 CFR 447 and 478), the sporting-purposes test, NFA limits, the Russia restrictions, ITAR temporary imports, importer marking and the federal excise tax — and the legal ways to pay less: USMCA, FTAs, Chapter 98, foreign-trade zones, rulings and drawback.
keywords: federal excise tax on firearms and ammunition

tariffEngineering.intro:
Firearms, their barrels and parts, and firearm ammunition need an **ATF import permit** before they can be imported: an approved **ATF Form 6** under the Arms Export Control Act and the Gun Control Act, presented to CBP at entry. ATF can approve only what the law allows — for example rifles and shotguns "particularly suitable for sporting purposes", not surplus military firearms — and machine guns and other National Firearms Act weapons only for government, research or dealer-sample use. **Firearms and ammunition made in or located in Russia are denied.** Importers must also mark each firearm and pay the **federal excise tax** when they sell it.

The ways to pay less duty are few, because most Chapter 93 base rates are low and the cost is the extra duty: **claim USMCA** on Canadian and Mexican goods, use an **FTA** where the base rate is the cost, enter **U.S. goods returned** under Chapter 98 (no Section 301 duty), hold goods in a **foreign-trade zone**, get a **binding ruling** on air guns, parts and scopes, and claim **drawback** on re-exports. For rifles with a scope, **declare the rifle and sight values separately** — the schedule requires it.

levers.title: Rifles with a scope: declare the rifle and the sight separately
levers.saves: Applies the sight rate only to the sight: 3.1% on the rifle + 13% on the sight (9303.30.80), 3.8% + 10% (9303.30.40) or 4.7% + 20% (9301.90.30), instead of a guess on the whole value
levers.appliesTo: Rifles imported with a telescopic sight mounted on them or designed to be mounted on them (9301.90.30, 9303.30.40, 9303.30.80); the sight is reported under its own statistical suffix (.10 or .05)
levers.document: Invoice values for the rifle and the sight; the sum must equal the value of the article (chapter 93 statistical note 1). The tariff calculator asks for both values.
levers.caveat: A sight imported without a rifle is not a Chapter 93 good (chapter note 1(d)): it is 9013.10.10 at 14.9% (NY N360004, N310885). The Section 301 duty is charged on the full value either way, and from the EU, Japan, Korea and Taiwan the 10%/12.5% total replaces the two-part rate when it is higher.

citations.label: HTSUS Chapter 93, note 1(d) and statistical note 1

levers.title: Claim USMCA on goods made in Canada or Mexico
levers.saves: The 10% Section 301 duty plus the base rate (up to 5.7%, or 14¢ each + 3% on pistols)
levers.appliesTo: All 67 lines, for goods that qualify as originating under USMCA — in 2025 mostly Canadian ammunition and gun parts and Mexican air guns, parts and ammunition
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer, in any format. Firearms of 9301–9304 qualify when made from materials of another chapter, or from parts of 9305 with at least 60% regional value content (transaction value) or 50% (net cost); parts of 9305 from any other heading; ammunition and swords (9306–9307) from any other chapter (General Note 11).
levers.caveat: Assembling imported parts of 9305 into a firearm needs the regional value content. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force. The ATF permit is still required.

levers.title: Claim an FTA rate where the base rate is the cost
levers.saves: The base rate: 14¢ each + 3% on pistols, 2.6% on shotguns, 3.1%–4.7% on rifles plus 10%–20% on sights, 3.5%–5.7% on stocks, parts, air rifles and truncheons, 2.7% on swords
levers.appliesTo: The 31 dutiable lines, for goods of Israel, Korea, Australia, Chile, Colombia, Peru, Panama, Jordan, Morocco, Bahrain, Oman, Singapore, CAFTA-DR, CBERA and AGOA countries
levers.document: Proof of origin under the program and the SPI on the entry line (IL, KR, AU, CL, CO, PE, PA, JO, MA, BH, OM, SG, P, E or D).
levers.caveat: FTA claims do not remove the 2026 Section 301 duty (U.S. note 52(a)): Israeli goods still pay 12.5%, and for Korea the 12.5% total already replaces the base rate. Ammunition (9306) is Free anyway. GSP (A, A+) has been expired since December 31, 2020.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Enter U.S. firearms returned, and repairs abroad, under Chapter 98
levers.saves: U.S. goods returned (9801.00.10) are Free and pay no Section 301 duty; repaired goods (9802.00.40/.50) pay duty only on the value of the repair
levers.appliesTo: Firearms and parts made in the United States and returned without having been advanced in value abroad, and U.S.-exported firearms repaired or altered abroad
levers.document: Proof of U.S. origin and export (19 CFR 10.1) or of the export for repair (19 CFR 10.8). ATF still requires a permit unless an exemption applies; a firearm the person took out of the United States may be brought back by that person (18 U.S.C. 925(d)(4)).
levers.caveat: The 2026 Section 301 duty still applies to the value of repairs entered under 9802.00.40/.50 (U.S. note 52(a)). Chapter 98 relief needs CBP to agree the entry is proper.

levers.title: Hold stock in a foreign-trade zone
levers.saves: Duty is paid only when goods leave the zone for U.S. consumption; goods re-exported from the zone pay none
levers.appliesTo: Firearms, parts and ammunition stored for later entry or re-export
levers.document: FTZ admission (CBP Form 214). ATF's rules do not treat bringing a firearm or ammunition into a foreign-trade zone for storage pending shipment abroad or later importation as "importation"; the ATF permit is needed when the goods are entered from the zone.
levers.caveat: ATF's May 8, 2026 proposal to extend this to customs-bonded warehouses and drop the "for storage" condition is not final. Duties, including the Section 301 duty, are due when goods are entered for consumption from the zone.

levers.title: Get a binding ruling before you import
levers.saves: Certainty where the line decides the rate: air rifles (9304.00.20, 3.9%) vs. other air guns (9304.00.40, Free), parts of air guns (9305.99.50, 3.9%) vs. other parts, scopes (9013.10.10, 14.9%) vs. rifle-plus-sight entries
levers.appliesTo: Airsoft and paintball guns, gun accessories (lights, lasers, mounts, holsters, cases), flash hiders, training swords and replicas
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the product, its materials and construction (19 CFR part 177). Published rulings show how CBP decides: N149835 (airsoft rifle, 9304.00.20), N140515 (airsoft pistol and shotgun, 9304.00.40), N095195 (paintball marker, 9304.00.40), N146796 (pellets 9306.29, plastic BBs 9306.90), N304308 (martial arts weapons, 9307).
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the transaction described. Parts "of general use" of base metal or plastics (screws, springs) are not gun parts (chapter note 1(b)).

citations.label: CBP ruling NY N146796 (air gun ammunition)

levers.title: Claim drawback when the goods are exported
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid, including Section 301 duties, on imported goods re-exported or used in exported goods
levers.appliesTo: All lines, when the imported goods or substitutes are exported or used in manufacturing exported goods (for example imported barrels and parts built into firearms for export)
levers.document: A drawback claim filed in ACE within 5 years of import, with records linking the import to the export. CBP has applied unused-merchandise drawback to imported pistols (HQ 228267).
levers.caveat: Only duties actually paid are refunded, not the excise tax; the export needs its own State Department or Commerce export authorization.

rules.title: Import permit: an approved ATF Form 6 (Part I) is needed before firearms, firearm barrels, ammunition and other articles on the U.S. Munitions Import List are imported; it lists the foreign seller, the manufacturer, type, caliber, model, quantity and unit cost, and the approved form is the permit. At release the permit holder files Form 6A with CBP, and for Category I and III articles a registered importer also gives CBP a copy of the exporting country's export license (or a certification that none is needed). Minor parts (not barrels, cylinders, receivers or breech mechanisms) worth $100 or less per transaction need no permit

What needs a permit: the U.S. Munitions Import List — Category I firearms (pistols, revolvers, rifles, combat and short-barreled shotguns, automatic weapons, silencers) and their parts, Category II artillery, Category III ammunition and its components (cartridge cases, bullets, primers; not shotgun shells), Category IV rockets, bombs and mines

What can be approved: firearms and ammunition for scientific or research use, unserviceable curios, firearms "generally recognized as particularly suitable for or readily adaptable to sporting purposes" (excluding surplus military firearms), and firearms the person took out of the U.S.; machine guns, short-barreled rifles and shotguns and other NFA weapons only for government use, research, or as samples

Gun Control Act definitions: a firearm expels a projectile by the action of an explosive (air, spring and gas guns are not firearms), antique firearms — made in or before 1898, and certain replicas — are excluded, and ammunition means cartridge cases, primers, bullets or propellent powder designed for use in a firearm

Proscribed countries: ATF denies permits for defense articles from the countries in 27 CFR 447.52(a), and for firearms and 7.62×25mm ammunition located or manufactured in Russia and other listed former Soviet states (447.52(b)); since September 7, 2021 all permanent-import permits for Russian firearms and ammunition (USMIL Categories I and III) are denied. BIS's Russia and Belarus rules (15 CFR 746.8) are export license requirements and do not govern imports

citations.label: 15 CFR 746.8 (BIS, exports to Russia and Belarus)

rules.title: Temporary imports of defense articles (for repair, exhibition or transit) are controlled by the State Department under the ITAR, not by an ATF permit; the policy of denial in 22 CFR 126.1 covers temporary imports originating in the listed countries, including Russia

Licensed importers must mark each imported firearm's frame or receiver with a serial number and their name and place of business (or a license-number prefix), and the firearm with its model, caliber or gauge, foreign manufacturer and country of manufacture; no one may assemble a semiautomatic rifle or shotgun that could not be imported from more than 10 of the listed imported parts

Federal excise tax on the importer's (or manufacturer's) sale: 10% of the sale price for pistols and revolvers, 11% for other firearms and for shells and cartridges. Parts and accessories sold separately are not taxed; makers and importers of fewer than 50 pistols, revolvers and firearms a year in all are exempt for those. It is a tax, not a customs duty
Country-of-origin marking on each article (or its container when the article cannot be marked), in English, legible and permanent enough to reach the ultimate purchaser

Report the Chapter 99 headings with the line: the 2026 Section 301 heading for the country (or 9903.05.93/.94 for USMCA goods), Brazil (9903.05.01), China List 4A (9903.88.15) on every line except 9305.99.40, and for Russia 9903.90.08 on its four subheadings

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 20, 30, 50 and 52

groups.label: Military weapons: artillery, rocket and grenade launchers, military rifles and shotguns, machine guns
groups.note: Military weapons need an ATF permit and are importable only within the 925(d) and NFA limits — machine guns only for government, research or dealer samples. Rifles with a scope (9301.90.30) pay 4.7% on the rifle + 20% on the sight.

groups.label: Revolvers and pistols
groups.note: Pistols and revolvers need an ATF Form 6 permit and must meet the sporting-purposes criteria; importers mark each one. The federal excise tax is 10% of the importer's sale price.

groups.label: Sporting and hunting shotguns and rifles, muzzle-loaders, blank-firing pistols, flare guns, captive-bolt and line-throwing guns
groups.note: Sporting shotguns and rifles need an ATF permit; rifles entered with a scope are valued in two parts (statistical note 1). Excise tax 11%. Flare guns, blank-firing pistols and captive-bolt guns are also here.

groups.label: Air guns, airsoft guns, paintball markers, spring guns, truncheons and other arms
groups.note: Air, spring and gas guns — airsoft guns and paintball markers too — do not fire by an explosive, so they are not firearms under the Gun Control Act. Classification between air rifles (3.9%) and other air guns (Free) decides the base rate; truncheons and other arms pay 5.7%.

groups.label: Gun parts and accessories: frames, receivers, barrels, stocks and other parts of firearms and air guns
groups.note: Frames, receivers, barrels and breech mechanisms need an ATF permit; other minor parts worth $100 or less per transaction do not. Parts of general use (screws, springs) are classified elsewhere.

groups.label: Ammunition: cartridges, shotgun shells, air gun pellets and BBs, paintballs, bombs, grenades, missiles and their parts
groups.note: Cartridges, cases, primers and bullets for firearms need an ATF permit; air gun pellets, BBs and paintballs are not firearm ammunition. Russian ammunition is denied. Excise tax 11% on shells and cartridges. All lines are Free at the base rate.

groups.label: Swords, cutlasses, bayonets, lances and similar arms, scabbards and sheaths
groups.note: Swords, bayonets and similar arms are not firearms or ammunition; they pay 2.7% and must be marked with their country of origin.

Import permits, the importability criteria, country restrictions and the excise tax are set by ATF, the State Department and the Treasury; check them with the agency before each shipment.

faqs.question: What does HTS Chapter 93 cover?
searchedAs: arms and ammunition; parts and accessories thereof tariff
faqs.answer: Arms and ammunition: military weapons (9301), revolvers and pistols (9302), sporting shotguns, rifles and other firearms (9303), air guns and other arms (9304), parts and accessories (9305), ammunition and munitions (9306), and swords and bayonets (9307) — 67 tariff lines. Percussion caps and flares (chapter 36), telescopic sights entered alone (chapter 90), bows and toys (chapter 95) and antiques (9705/9706) are classified elsewhere.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for firearms — pistols, rifles and shotguns?
faqs.answer: Pistols and revolvers are 9302.00.00 (14¢ each + 3%). Sporting and hunting shotguns are 9303.20.00 (2.6%) and sporting rifles 9303.30 (3.8% or 3.1% on the rifle plus 10% or 13% on any scope). Muzzle-loaders are 9303.10 (Free), and military rifles, shotguns and machine guns 9301.90.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for ammunition and cartridges?
faqs.answer: Heading 9306, all Free at the base rate: shotgun cartridges 9306.21, their parts and air gun pellets 9306.29, rifle and pistol cartridges and empty cases 9306.30.41 (.22 caliber under suffix 10), other cartridge parts 9306.30.80, and bombs, grenades, missiles, other projectiles and plastic BBs 9306.90 (NY N146796). The duty is the country's extra duty: 10% from the UK or the EU, 12.5% from Türkiye, 37.5% from Brazil.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for gun parts and accessories?
faqs.answer: Heading 9305. Pistol parts are 9305.10 — frames, receivers and other parts of 9302 pistols 4.2%. Shotgun and rifle parts are 9305.20 — rifle stocks 3.5%, shotgun barrels and other parts Free. Parts of military weapons (9305.91) are Free; parts of air guns 3.9% and other parts 2.9% (9305.99). Screws, springs and other parts of general use are classified by their material (chapter note 1(b)).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for a rifle scope, and how is a rifle with a scope taxed?
faqs.answer: A scope imported on its own is 9013.10.10 (14.9%; NY N360004). A scope mounted on the rifle or entered with it stays with the rifle: the rifle line charges, for example, 3.1% on the rifle's value + 13% on the sight's value (9303.30.80). The importer reports the two values under separate statistical suffixes, and they must add up to the article's value (statistical note 1).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for air guns, airsoft guns and paintball markers?
faqs.answer: Spring, air and gas guns are 9304.00: rifles 9304.00.20 (3.9%; an airsoft rifle, NY N149835), other air guns 9304.00.40 (Free; airsoft pistols and shotguns, NY N140515; paintball markers, NY N095195). Their parts are 9305.99.50 (3.9%), pellets 9306.29 and plastic BBs and paintballs 9306.90.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for a sword?
faqs.answer: Swords, cutlasses, bayonets, lances, their parts, scabbards and sheaths are 9307.00.00 at 2.7% (karate sai, NY N304308). Toy swords are chapter 95 goods, and a wooden martial arts training sword was classified in 9506.99.60 (NY N326170). From China a sword pays 22.7% in total.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on guns and ammunition in 2026?
faqs.answer: Yes. Since July 24, 2026 the Section 301 tariff on 60 economies reaches every Chapter 93 line, with no exemption list: 10% in total for EU and Taiwanese goods, 12.5% in total for Japan and South Korea, the base rate plus 12.5% for Türkiye and Israel, plus 10% for the UK, plus 37.5% for Brazil and plus 20% for China. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt. The IEEPA tariffs ended February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: What do firearms and ammunition from Türkiye, Italy, Austria, Brazil and Canada pay?
faqs.answer: Turkish shotguns 15.1%, pistols 14¢ each + 15.5%, 9mm ammunition 12.5%. Italian shotguns and Austrian pistols 10% in total. Brazilian pistols 14¢ each + 40.5%, ammunition 37.5%. Canadian goods: free with a USMCA claim, otherwise the base rate plus 10%.

faqs.question: Do I need an ATF Form 6 to import firearms or ammunition?
searchedAs: can you import firearms into the us
importing a gun into the us
faqs.answer: Yes, for firearms, firearm barrels, ammunition and most parts on the U.S. Munitions Import List: ATF must approve a Form 6 (Part I) application, and the approved form is the permit. At release from CBP the permit holder files Form 6A. Only a licensed importer may import firearms or ammunition as a business, and ATF can approve only what 18 U.S.C. 925(d) allows, such as firearms particularly suitable for sporting purposes.

faqs.question: Can I bring my own firearm back into the U.S. after a trip abroad?
searchedAs: bringing firearms into the us from canada
atf form 6 temporary importation of firearms
faqs.answer: Yes, if you can show CBP that you took it out of the United States: register it on CBP Form 4457 before departure, or keep a bill of sale or other document showing you acquired it in the U.S. (27 CFR 478.115(a)). No import permit is needed for that firearm.

faqs.question: What is the federal excise tax on firearms and ammunition?
searchedAs: federal excise tax on firearms and ammunition
faqs.answer: 10% of the sale price for pistols and revolvers and 11% for other firearms and for shells and cartridges (26 U.S.C. 4181), owed by the manufacturer, producer or importer on its sale. Makers and importers of fewer than 50 firearms a year in all are exempt for firearms, and sales to the military are exempt. It is a tax, not a customs duty.

faqs.question: Is Russian ammunition banned from import?
searchedAs: is russian ammo still being imported
faqs.answer: Yes. Since September 7, 2021 ATF must deny permits to permanently import firearms and ammunition manufactured or located in Russia, under a State Department sanction, and ATF's regulation already barred most Russian firearms (27 CFR 447.52). U.S. imports from Russia fell from $183M in 2021 to under $0.3M a year since 2023. ATF proposed in May 2026 to keep Russia on its list while dropping other former Soviet states.

faqs.question: Does ITAR apply to imports of firearms?
faqs.answer: Permanent imports of firearms and ammunition are controlled by ATF under the Arms Export Control Act (27 CFR part 447, the U.S. Munitions Import List). Temporary imports — for repair, exhibition or return — fall under the State Department's ITAR, including its exemptions in 22 CFR 123.4 and the country policy of 22 CFR 126.1.

faqs.question: How much arms and ammunition does the U.S. import, and from where?
faqs.answer: $3.86B of Chapter 93 goods in 2025, down 13.3% from $4.45B in 2024. Ammunition was $1.34B, pistols $660M, shotguns $347M, rifles $254M and gun parts $1.02B. Türkiye ($419M), the UK ($389M), Italy ($366M), Germany ($318M) and Austria ($249M) were the largest suppliers.
